about: Head injury danger signs, sudden cardiac arrest, seizures, altitude illness, burns, low blood sugar and sepsis. Written from CDC and Ready.gov pages (public domain), in plain words, adding nothing the source doesn't say. Not reviewed by a medical professional.

entries.title: concussion assessment
entries.text: After a bump, blow or jolt to the head, call 911 or go to an emergency department right away if the person: has a headache that gets worse and doesn't go away; has weakness, numbness, poor coordination, convulsions or seizures; vomits repeatedly; has slurred speech or unusual behavior; has one pupil larger than the other; can't recognize people or places, or becomes confused, restless or agitated; passes out, looks very drowsy or can't be woken. For a child, also if they won't stop crying and can't be consoled, or won't nurse or eat. Common concussion symptoms otherwise: headache, dizziness or balance problems, nausea or vomiting early on, being bothered by light or noise, vision problems, tiredness, feeling foggy or slowed down, trouble concentrating or remembering, irritability, sadness or anxiety, and sleeping more or less than usual.

source.name: CDC, Symptoms of Mild TBI and Concussion

entries.title: sudden cardiac arrest
entries.text: Signs of sudden cardiac arrest (the same in children and adults): sudden collapse and loss of consciousness; not breathing, or only gasping; no response to shouting or shaking; no pulse. Call 911 immediately and start CPR. Send someone to find an AED (automated external defibrillator), or get one yourself when it's safe; most AEDs can be used on adults and on children over 8. Keep doing CPR until medical professionals take over or the person starts breathing on their own.

source.name: CDC, About Sudden Cardiac Arrest in Children and Youth

entries.title: seizure first aid
entries.text: During a seizure: keep yourself and others calm and stay with the person. Clear away anything nearby that could hurt them. If they're lying down, turn them gently on their side with the mouth pointing to the ground. Time the seizure. Don't hold them down or stop their movements, don't put anything in their mouth, don't give mouth-to-mouth breaths, and don't give food or water until they're fully alert. Call 911 if: the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes; another seizure follows soon after; they have trouble breathing or waking afterwards; it happens in water; they're injured; it's their first seizure; they have diabetes and lose consciousness; or they're pregnant.

entries.title: altitude sickness recognition
entries.text: Acute mountain sickness, the mildest form: headache, tiredness, poor appetite, nausea, vomiting. High-altitude cerebral edema (HACE), more serious: extreme tiredness, drowsiness, confusion, loss of coordination. High-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), which can quickly become life-threatening: shortness of breath, weakness, cough. Anyone with altitude illness shouldn't go higher until the symptoms are gone. If symptoms get worse while resting, go to a lower elevation. With HACE or HAPE, the person must immediately move, or be moved, to a lower elevation; HAPE will likely need oxygen. Prevention: don't go from low elevation to above 9,000 feet (2,750 m) in one day; if possible spend a few days at 8,000-9,000 feet first; above 9,000 feet, raise where you sleep by no more than 1,600 feet a day; and for every 3,300 feet you climb, spend an extra day at that elevation.

source.name: CDC Travelers' Health, Travel to High Altitudes

entries.title: burns treatment
entries.text: Minor burns: hold the burned skin under cool running water (not cold water or ice, which can injure it more) for 10 to 15 minutes, until it's less painful, especially for a chemical burn. Without running water, soak it in a cool water bath for five minutes. Remove clothing, diapers, jewelry and metal from the burned area. Don't break blisters; an opened blister can get infected. You may put on a thin layer of petroleum jelly or aloe vera, but not cream, lotion, oil, cortisone, butter or egg white. Cover it with sterile non-stick gauze, lightly taped or wrapped, and change the dressing once a day. See a doctor, call 911 or go to the hospital if the burn is larger than two inches; if it's dark red and glossy with a lot of blistering, or dry and leathery with white, brown or black patches; or if it came from a fire, an electrical wire or socket, or chemicals. These need immediate medical attention. Contact a provider for signs of infection: more pain, redness, swelling, discharge, fever, swollen lymph nodes or a red streak from the burn.

entries.title: low blood sugar
entries.text: Blood sugar below 70 mg/dL is low; below 55 mg/dL is severely low. The 15-15 rule: have 15 grams of carbs, wait 15 minutes, and check blood sugar again; if it's still below 70 mg/dL, repeat. 15 grams of carbs is: 4 ounces (half a cup) of juice or regular (not diet) soda; 1 tablespoon of sugar, honey or syrup; 3-4 glucose tablets or 1 dose of glucose gel (follow the instructions); or hard candies, jellybeans or gumdrops (see the label for how many). Once it's back up, eat a snack or meal with protein and carbs. Young children, especially infants and toddlers, may need less than 15 grams; ask their doctor how much. Injectable glucagon is the best treatment for severely low blood sugar: someone who has passed out usually wakes within 15 minutes; if not, give one more dose. Contact a doctor for emergency treatment immediately after a glucagon injection.

source.name: CDC, Treatment of Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia)

entries.title: sepsis recognition
entries.text: Sepsis is the body's extreme response to an infection, and a life-threatening medical emergency: without fast treatment it can quickly lead to tissue damage, organ failure and death, so act fast. A person with sepsis might have one or more of: clammy or sweaty skin; confusion or disorientation; extreme pain or discomfort; fever, shivering or feeling very cold; a high heart rate or weak pulse; shortness of breath. Anyone can develop sepsis.
